title: Sesame Street Transforms Chappell Roan’s ‘Hot to Go!’ Into the Potty-Training Anthem ‘Got to Go,’ With Lead Vocals From Cookie Monster
description: Sesame Street has a half-century-long tradition of legendary musical guests and innovative adaptations: from Stevie Wonder’s iconic performance in t
body:
Sesame Street has a half-century-long tradition of legendary musical guests and innovative adaptations: from Stevie Wonder’s iconic performance in the early ‘70s to Tony Bennett retrofitting his timeless classic “Fly Me to the Moon” to be a story about the show’s worm character Slimy on an expedition to the moon (“Slimy to the Moon,” of course); from the Fugees’ inclusion anthem “Just Happy to Be Me” to blues legend B.B. King singing an ode to the letter that has meant so much to his career; from Smokey Robinson getting groped by the letter “U” for “U Really Got a Hold on Me” to — this writer’s personal favorite — opera legend Marilyn Horne trilling an orchestral version of “C Is for Cookie” on an elaborate mock-Egyptian set while wearing a tiara adorned with a bouncing cookie.
	

	And some 57 years after the show premiered, its brilliant combination of education, musicality and humor continues: In a newly released video, they transform Chappell Roan’s “Hot to Go” into a potty-training anthem called “Got to Go” with inimitable lead vocals from the Cookie Monster.




	It’s a note-for-note rendition too, complete with the song’s chanted middle section from guest vocalists Elmo and Abby Cadabby. And although we don’t get to see Muppets doing the world-famous hand-gestures spelling out the song’s title, instead we get singing letters spelling out POTTY.

	Cookie Monster intones in his trademark broken English:

	“Stop and listen to me body/ It’s saying that it’s time for potty,There’s a growing feeling in my tummy, that me gotta go pee, me gotta go pee…There they go again, now me legs are grooving/ There might be a mess if me don’t get movin’…
	

	“P-O-T-T-Y, woah-oh, your body knows when you’ve got to go…”

	It even starts with a talking number one and two. 

	Contacted by Variety, a rep for Chappell Roan said the singer had no comment. Indeed, none was necessary: Granting permission for her and cowriter/producer Dan Nigro’s song to be used in such an amusing and imaginatively instructive way — for young children, no less — is a statement in itself.

schema.headline: Sesame Street Transforms Chappell Roan’s ‘Hot to Go!’ Into the Potty-Training Anthem ‘Got to Go,’ With Lead Vocals From Cookie Monster

title: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Was Inspired by Universal Monsters and Hammer Horror Movies
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom,” now in theaters.

	Shaun the Sheep is back for h
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom,” now in theaters.

	Shaun the Sheep is back for his third feature-length film, “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.” This time around, Shaun and his fellow sheep are getting ready for Halloween — except, the pumpkin patch has a problem. When Shaun attempts to fix it, things go awry as he creates a growth formula that transforms the farmer into a terrorizing, hairy beast.
	

	The film contains very little dialogue, but it brims with visual gags and nods that Aardman’s stop-motion animators cleverly crammed in: “Psycho,” “Star Wars” and even “The Shining” (a pub is called The Shine Inn). However, the biggest influences behind the storytelling came from classic Universal monsters and the Hammer Film Productions horrors.


	Speaking with Variety, the film’s directors Steve Cox and Matthew Walker, explained that the initial idea was for it to be a Valentine’s Day special. “It was always the idea of the farmer having a relationship with someone, but then at some point, the idea of a monster came up,” says Walker. “And the ideas got combined at some point. Then the natural progression of that was it being a Halloween special.”

	As the ideas evolved, the story of Shaun being a mad scientist emerged as an early concept the team loved. Aardman’s stop-motion studio is no stranger to doing monster movies, having previously produced “Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit.” If they were going to tackle another monster movie, they wanted it to look completely different.
	

	Cox explains the monster needed to have a very distinctive silhouette. To achieve this, they spent time carefully designing the character. Cox says, “We knew that it was going to be created from hair, because it’s obviously the farmer. Spoiler alert! With all the hair growing out from his sides, his beard and going up into these bushy tufts at the top. We love the fact that he’s got this great, distinctive, almost-horns, as he’s coming over the hill.”

	Given the farmer has ginger hair, that allowed them to visually integrate him into the orange world of pumpkins and blood-red sunsets. Fox says, “That allowed us to up the level of saturation in this film.”

	The inspirations of “Wolfman” and “Frankenstein” are obvious to any fan of Universal monsters. “We took our visual language from the films that Matt and I grew up with in the ‘80s,” Cox says as he also cites “Ghostbusters,” “Indiana Jones” and “The Goonies” as references. He adds, “But our story started in the kind of Universal monsters and Hammer horror [world].”

	Cox admits that leaning into horror gags proved to be a challenge, given the franchise’s family-friendly nature. “We had to bring things in do our own take on them and make it family-friendly because we didn’t want to alienate an audience.”

	Among the tropes of the genre were spooky woods, shadows, creaky branches and misty docks — all elements that could create jump scares, but of a friendly nature. One scene features the flock of sheep in the house being chased, with the question of where would they hide? They end up in the bathroom, which leads to a “Psycho” gag.

	Walker explains all of those references and ideas come from the story and the characters. “It always happened very organically.”

	Aardman continues to use stop-motion technology to tell the stories of its beloved characters, and while Walker says many aspects of the studio’s pipeline have stayed the same, some technology has evolved. “We’re using digital still cameras now rather than film.” And while the use of digital effects in films has increased, Walker says, “We always try and do as much as we can in camera.”

	As for their knack for telling stories without dialogue, it still proves to be challenging, particularly when telling an emotional story. The film’s subplot is a love story between the farmer and the vet, except the growth potion complicates the farmer’s attraction. Similarly, the sheep have solid heads, which limits facial expressions. Walker explains that with the sheep, any expression has to come through their body language and eyebrows and eye movements and mouths. The farmer is even more difficult because he doesn’t even have eyeballs — he’s just glasses and a mouth. But we have such brilliant animators that whatever’s in the storyboards, they’ll be able to find a way to convey those emotions.”

schema.headline: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Was Inspired by Universal Monsters and Hammer Horror Movies

title: ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization
description: There’s nothing more distressing in “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ than the unflinching closeups of the author’s wounded body in th
body:
There’s nothing more distressing in “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ than the unflinching closeups of the author’s wounded body in the days and weeks after August 12, 2022, when he was repeatedly stabbed while on stage at a literary festival in upstate New York. The camera lingers over his mangled hand and the train-track of stitches running up his belly. His right eye is a bloodied bulge. The power of Alex Gibney’s documentary, which premiered at Sundance, lies in Rushdie’s decision to showcase his scars — quite literally, by sharing footage that his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths shot throughout his time in the hospital. It’s a visceral complement to what is otherwise a solid, if standard, profile of the author from Gibney, the Oscar- and Emmy-winner known for churning out reliably comprehensive, reporter-style investigations of power and politics.
	

	In Gibney’s upcoming “Musk,” an HBO-produced Elon Musk mega-doc that showed at Venice, the SpaceX and Tesla overlord is an AI-generated talking head. Thankfully no such uncanny simulations are in play here. The Indian-born writer has control of the mic from the get-go with running voiceover narration that starts the film alongside a feverish recreation of the attack visualized from Rushdie’s point of view: Blinding stage lights turn his assailant, a New Jersey man by the name of Hadi Matar, into a shadowy mass, and each jab of the knife is heard as a fleshy thud. Matar is only mentioned by name once. In Rushdie’s retelling, he becomes a symbol for the punishing incursions upon his life and liberties since the publication of his 1988 novel “The Satanic Verses” scandalized the masses and put a target on his head, courtesy of a fatwa issued by Ayatollah Khomeini, then the Supreme ruler of Iran.
	

	Wondering why he didn’t fight back or run away, Rushdie moves into an extended reflection on his relationship to death and fatalism. In the present thread, we follow his recovery through Griffiths’ tenderly diaristic documentation, which includes, at one point, a call from family friend Wes Anderson. Meanwhile Gibney employs archival news footage and old on-camera interviews with Rushdie to take us back to his identity-crisis-riddled early years between India and his adopted home of London, and the emotional abuse he suffered while living with his alcoholic father. But for the most part, Gibney keeps to the events after 1988, when Rushdie’s Islam-inspired magical realist tome became the flashpoint for a fiery debate over free speech and creative freedom.

	Excerpts from the novel are accompanied by scratchy animated renderings of the story — about two Indian-Muslim men living in London who undergo spiritual upheavals after surviving a plane crash — that echo Rushdie’s existential musings and emphasize the work as a product of his imagination. It’s a way of highlighting the absurdity of the violent response from orthodox Muslim communities —  all this rage for a story? — and more generally, the dangers that religious extremism poses to civil society. When Ayatollah Khomeini called for Rushdie’s righteous assassination in 1989, protests and book burnings broke out in the U.K., Pakistan and India; elsewhere, bookstores were destroyed, editorial offices torched, and Rushdie’s Japanese translator, Hitoshi Agarashi, was murdered. These aren’t breaking revelations for what is — for a certain generation, at least — one of the late 20th century’s most shocking and widely-discussed controversies.

	But lest we dismiss these events as contained to the past, the 2022 assault stands as a reminder that artistic expression remains as frighteningly vulnerable as Rushdie’s brutalized body. That message might feel obvious for anyone even remotely tapped into the American news cycle, but it’s given a weighty (if obligatorily sentimental) personal touch by the resilient Rushdie and his support system, led by the tenacious Griffiths — his rock against a seemingly neverending saga.

schema.headline: ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization

title: Jamie XX Plays Live Accompaniment to Doug Aitken’s ‘Lightscape’ Show at the Shed in New York
description: Doug Aitken’s “Lightscape” is a seven-screen, film-based installation that just completed a run at the Shed’s 12,000-sq.-ft. Darla Moore Gallery tha
body:
Doug Aitken’s “Lightscape” is a seven-screen, film-based installation that just completed a run at the Shed’s 12,000-sq.-ft. Darla Moore Gallery that completed its run earlier this week, but as part of the venue’s annual invite-only gala on Thursday night, Jamie XX played a live score as the images rolled by, in an immersive setting of sound and vision.

	Aitken’s 65-minute installation features multiple characters — played by Natasha Lyonne, Beck, members of the Los Angeles Dance Project and more — moving through settings across America, from deserts and remote mountains to factories and highways. The images are vaguely Wim Wenders-esque, and although several of the scenes feature more than one person, the characters rarely interact. In a brief conversation with Variety after the show, Aitken said that, broadly speaking, the installation was a reflection of the isolation and dissocations people can feel in modern society.
	



	

					Lightscape (minus audience)
	



	Jamie XX’s solo work is electronic in nature but is often more centered around melody than the music of many of his contemporaries. While his score for this particular show was more atmospheric and less song-based than his excellent 2024 album “In Waves,” the hallmarks of his sound remained — unusual juxtapositions of voices and beats, and sound manipulation that the audience, which was free to talk right up to the console behind which he and his equipment were creating the sounds, was able to watch in real time. Surprisingly, the set ended with “Doot Doot,” a low-key 1983 dance song by Welsh synth-pop outfit Freur (which featured two future members of Underworld) that was popular with new-wave DJs during that era.
	

	While on certain nights during the summer the installation featured live improvised performances from the Los Angeles Master Chorale, William Basinski, Suzanne Ciani and the Sun Ra Arkestra, Jamie told Variety that he and Aitken had been collaborating on the project for months, and the music he prepared for this performance had been recorded, although he wasn’t sure whether it will be released. Whether or not it is, the performance suggests that he has considerable potential as a film composer.  



	

					Jamie XX (left) with Doug Aitken (Photo: Alexis Buatti-Ramos)

schema.headline: Jamie XX Plays Live Accompaniment to Doug Aitken’s ‘Lightscape’ Show at the Shed in New York

title: How to Stream Every Season of ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Online
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Olivia Be
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Olivia Benson has been keeping New York safe for nearly three decades — and Hulu has enough “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” to keep viewers occupied for nearly as long.

	Ahead of the procedural’s Season 28 premiere on Oct. 8, all 27 previously aired seasons of Dick Wolf’s long-running NBC drama are currently available to stream on Hulu, totaling 589 episodes. Hulu plans currently start at $11.99 per month.


	Season 28 premieres Thursday, Oct. 8 on NBC. Viewers who want to watch new episodes live without traditional cable can do so through Hulu + Live TV, which carries NBC in participating markets and currently starts at $89.99 per month. New Season 28 episodes will also be available to stream on Peacock the day after their NBC broadcast.
	

	The new season once again finds Mariska Hargitay at the center of the action as Capt. Olivia Benson, a role she has played since SVU first premiered in 1999. Ice-T returns as Sgt. Odafin “Fin” Tutuola, alongside Kelli Giddish as Amanda Rollins, Peter Scanavino as Sonny Carisi, Kevin Kane as Terry Bruno and Aimé Donna Kelly as Renee Curry.

	Season 28 is shaping up to be a particularly consequential one for Benson. Showrunner Michele Fazekas has teased a season-long storyline examining the toll that decades of working Special Victims cases has taken on the veteran captain. She’ll also get a new sounding board in “Succession” star J. Smith-Cameron, who joins the season in a recurring role as Gwen. “SVU” will also reach its 600th episode during Season 28 and Fazekas has hinted that the landmark episode could also bring a familiar face back into Benson’s orbit.
	

	Hargitay, meanwhile, enters the season after an especially busy year outside the squad room. The actor hosted the 78th Emmy Awards on Sept. 14 and used the gig to stage an elaborate SVU sketch featuring Ice-T, Giddish and the rest of the cast — plus a surprise appearance from longtime superfan Taylor Swift as a rookie detective. Hargitay has also recently spoken about wanting to continue playing Benson through a potential 30th season.

	Stream every season of “SVU” on Hulu here.

schema.headline: How to Stream Every Season of ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Online

title: Amazon Moves to Toss ‘Criminal’ Production Assistant’s Harassment Suit
description: Amazon MGM has filed a motion to throw out a suit brought by a production assistant on the upcoming series “Criminal,” saying that his claim that th
body:
Amazon MGM has filed a motion to throw out a suit brought by a production assistant on the upcoming series “Criminal,” saying that his claim that the showrunner pointed a gun at him is “pure invention.”

	The plaintiff, Ijaaz Noohu, filed the suit two weeks ago, alleging he was subject to racial and sexual harassment. Among other things, Noohu accused showrunner Ed Brubaker of rubbing his back and of making comments about running his hands through Noohu’s hair.
	

	The complaint also alleged that Noohu was asked whether he supports Hamas, and was subjected to racial stereotypes about curry, mathematical ability and “Tiger Moms.” The most sensational allegation, offered with scant detail, was that Brubaker once pointed a functional firearm at him and pulled the trigger.


	In its demurrer filed on Thursday, Amazon MGM says it has no record of any report of the firearm incident, and accuses Noohu of making it up.

	The demurrer describes Noohu as “an opportunist, not a victim,” and quotes from an email Noohu sent in 2024, pitching himself for a promotion to be the show’s executive producer, saying it would “make the show better.”

	Amazon’s lawyers also state that Noohu never raised a complaint of harassment or discrimination during his work on the show.

	“His contemporaneous emails and texts — including the one begging to keep working closely with Brubaker, his supposed harasser — breathe not a word of harassment, discrimination, or distress,” the demurrer states. “Nor did Noohu ever hold himself out as religious or as sensitive to sexual content on a production he knew was based on mature, adult subject matter as a matter of course.”
	

	The demurrer also states that it is implausible that anyone would have pointed a gun at Noohu and pulled the trigger without it being reported.

	“Had that happened, every person in the room, Noohu included, had a duty to report it, and in a post-‘Rust’ industry on high alert to firearms, someone would have. No one did. Defendants first learned of the supposed incident when Noohu reemerged peddling the story and demanding a payday.”

	Amazon also alleges that Noohu sat on his allegations for nearly two years, until the beginning of the press tour for “Criminal,” in order to achieve maximum leverage.

schema.headline: Amazon Moves to Toss ‘Criminal’ Production Assistant’s Harassment Suit

title: HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Music Will Be ‘As Far Away as Possible’ From the Movies; Hans Zimmer Says ‘I Can’t Write Like John Williams’
description: While the trailers HBO has released for its upcoming “Harry Potter” reboot share a lot of similarities with the original movies, the music will be t
body:
While the trailers HBO has released for its upcoming “Harry Potter” reboot share a lot of similarities with the original movies, the music will be totally different.

	In an interview with Collider, Hans Zimmer spoke about the how intimidating it was to follow the footsteps of iconic composer John Williams. “Harry Potter” marks Zimmer’s second project based on IP that Williams had already written for — he previously scored Zack Snyder’s 2013 Superman film “Man of Steel” after Williams had composed for the 1978 “Superman” film and its 1980 sequel.
	

	When asked about whether his “Harry Potter” music would be similar to Williams’, Zimmer pointed to his experience on “Man of Steel,” saying, “I can’t write like John Williams, but even if I could, I would try to stay away as far as possible and try to be original.”


	“When I was doing ‘Man of Steel,’ which, of course, is Superman, for three months I was running around going, ‘I don’t know. I can’t do this. I can’t do this because it’s John Williams. John Williams is — it’s brilliant! It’s brilliant!'” Zimmer said, as Williams had composed the score for  He went on to explain that Christopher Nolan was a producer on “Man of Steel” and pushed Zack Snyder to check on Zimmer’s progress. “Zack phoned me and said, ‘Can I come down?’ I go, ‘I don’t really have anything,’ and he goes, ‘Well, I’ll be there on Tuesday.’ So I came up with a tune, but I still was incredibly worried about it.”

	Zimmer continued, “Zack just said the simplest thing to me. He said, ‘Hans, it was just a movie. This is just a movie.’ And that was so liberating. It’s just a movie, and my life is all about making music for movies, which I do because I love it. I love the movies, and I love having fun with it.”
	

	Williams was the composer on the first three “Harry Potter” films, which were released between 2001 and 2004. “Hedwig’s Theme,” the musical motif most commonly associated with the IP, appears in all seven films and is widely considered one of the greatest pieces of film music ever.

	Season 1 of the “Harry Potter” reboot will debut on HBO near Christmas. See trailers for the new series here and here.

schema.headline: HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Music Will Be ‘As Far Away as Possible’ From the Movies; Hans Zimmer Says ‘I Can’t Write Like John Williams’

title: Donald Trump Says He’s Banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico From the White House ‘Effective Immediately’ Because of ‘Their Constant Fake News’
description: President Donald Trump said he is immediately banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, slamming the news outlets for their “fake news”
body:
President Donald Trump said he is immediately banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, slamming the news outlets for their “fake news” reporting.

	On Friday afternoon, Trump wrote on social media, “I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW (who recently changed their name from MSNBC due to lack of viewership and credibility!), and Politico (The recipients of an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription, an All Time Record, directly from the United States Government, under Crooked Joe Biden, in order to keep them ‘alive.’ Seems like corruption to me!), from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” 
	

	Trump added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”


	In a statement Friday, CNN said, “CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”

	Variety has reached out to MS NOW and Politico for comment.

	In his social media post, Trump did not indicate what triggered his decision to declare that the three news outlets would no longer be welcome at the White House. Variety has asked the White House for clarification.
	

	In comments during a press briefing in the Oval Office Friday, Trump said his ban was not prompted by any particular story, but spurred by the “cumulative” tone of the coverage — in other words, the president would like to see more positive coverage about him and his administration.

	“They purposely write negative news,” Trump told reporters. “And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.”

	Asked which news outlets Trump may be consider banning next from the White House, he cited the New York Times and the Washington Post, saying, “They’re disgusting.”

	Trump’s reference to U.S. government subscriptions to Politico is based on data from USAspending.gov, a government website that tracks federal spending, which showed government agencies collectively spent more than $8 million combined in payments for Politico subscriptions and products in 2024, as reported by CBS News.

	Free-speech organizations and press groups decried Trump’s announcement, and there are likely to be legal challenges if Trump carries through on the ban.

	 “The National Press Club condemns President Trump’s declaration on Truth Social that he plans to immediately ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House,” National Press Club president Mark Schoeff Jr. said in a statement. “Banning news organizations from the White House based on the administration’s disapproval of their coverage is a clear attempt to control which voices are allowed to witness and report on the exercise of presidential power. Every American should understand what is at stake. If implemented, this ban would mark an unprecedented assault on press freedom.”

	Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF), commented, “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”

	Last year, the White House blocked AP staffers from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other areas after the news service continued referring to the body of water on the southeastern periphery of the North America as the Gulf of Mexico, after Trump decreed on his first day back in office in 2025 that henceforth it should be known as the “Gulf of America.” The AP sued over the shoutout, but an appeals court found that the White House’s ban of the news outlet was not a First Amendment violation.
	

	A study released this week by the Pew Research Center found 44% of all U.S. adults say the press has become less free during the second Trump administration, compared with 12% who say it has become more free. Opinions split dramatically based on party affiliation: 72% of Democrats say the press has become less free since Trump’s return to office, compared with 15% of Republicans, according to the study.

schema.headline: Donald Trump Says He’s Banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico From the White House ‘Effective Immediately’ Because of ‘Their Constant Fake News’

title: Navigating AI, Super-Serving Audiences, Engaging the Creator Economy and More at Variety’s 2026 Entertainment and Technology Summit
description: Executives, marketing professionals, entrepreneurs and creators across the field of film, television and gaming came together for a day of keynote s
body:
Executives, marketing professionals, entrepreneurs and creators across the field of film, television and gaming came together for a day of keynote speakers, panels and networking on Thursday for the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY.

	Industry professionals from Blumhouse Atomic Monster, Sony, Warner Bros., Mattel, Reddit and more spoke about navigating AI, engaging fandom, the creator economy and the future of the entertainment industry during the event at the Beverly Hills Four Seasons Hotel.
	

	A keynote conversation with Nick Kroll touched on his desire for productions to shoot in Los Angeles and his upcoming Netflix comedy series “A Hundred Percent.”

	Bill Hader spoke in a keynote conversation about voicing Cat in the Hat and why young people are resistant to AI.

	Director, writer and producer James Wan, of Blumhouse Atomic Monster, addressed the accessibility to technology that allows the breakout success of YouTube creators on films like “Obsession” and “Backrooms,” both of which Atomic Monster Blumhouse had a hand in.

	Keith Le Goy, Sony’s TV chief, talked about how the company has activated its incredibly engaged audience. Nintendo of America president and COO Devon Pritchard discussed the Switch 2 and “Legend of Zelda” projects, including a film collaboration with Sony Pictures.

	Other sessions included top media executives from NBCUniversal Entertainment, Crunchyroll, Hulu and more, who spoke about super-serving audiences and the dangers of AI slop. Panelists in another session discussed the possibilities for AI as a catalyst for communal engagement. Marketing professionals discussed how creators and platforms fuel fandom, and entertainment leaders talked about AI’s place in the industry.
	

	Read below for a few key takeaways from the 2026 Entertainment and Technology Summit:

	When Stories Speak: Reaching Audiences in the Next Era of Entertainment

	Nancy Hall, U.S. CEO at WPP Media, talked about how to know when something resonates with audiences between short-form, long-form and live experiences. “The red thread of these formats and of telling stories in this way is making them participatory, giving people the opportunity to respond to them, to talk about them, to shape them, to share them, and that’s what makes stories culture and not just content,” she said.

	The conversation, moderated by Variety editor-in-chief Cynthia Littleton, discussed how to turn buzz into business.


	LISTEN to Turning Buzz into Business With WPP Media’s Nancy Hall and Audible’s Tom McKenna on Variety’s “Strictly Business” podcast

	Tom McKenna, Audible global head of media, operations and business development, highlighted the company’s launch of its new brand, which focuses on stories that speak to its audience.


	“We’re taking things that are everyday moments and making them more valuable,” he said. “It’s about how Audible enriches a listener’s life.”

	McKenna and Hall talked about the unique advertising Audible has engaged this year, like an ad that took TikTok out of a phone and onto a building in Times Square. Hall said the brands that think of media as a “creative canvas” are the ones that break through the “sea of sameness.”

	Looking to the future, McKenna said those who are willing to take risks will be the ones who succeed. Hall said modern marketing is rooted in science and art. “We have to market today to two different entities,” she said. “We have to ensure that humans desire us, but that machines recommend us.”

	The Future of IRL: Trends in Event and Experiential Entertainment

	Senior vice president of global experiences for Paramount Marie Marks highlighted hospitality’s ability to offer something no other format can offer. A hotel where families stay with IP for days is a “full flywheel of experiences” that is powerful when done right.

	The growing Nickelodeon hotel business has 1,000 rooms in the market and another 2,000 in development globally. “A big learning for us was actually that the IP alone is not enough,” Marks said. “The underlying product has to be exceptional. One’s not enough without the other.”

	A brand like Hallmark is largely associated with one season, and in recent years has launched cruises and in-person experiences.

	President of Hallmark Media and chief brand officer Darren Abbott said the company has found success in expanding because as consumers want to spend more time at the holidays, they do so by spending more time with Hallmark.

	Natalia Premovic, chief consumer products and experiences officer at Mattel, attended an in-person Uno event in Los Angeles in August. She said attendees connected over the game strategy with people they might not have met otherwise.
	

	Premovic and Marks have seen these experiences expand the fanbase across generations.

	“No longer does the screen have to be the end of the interaction with the IP,” Marks said. “Increasingly so, it’s really just becoming the beginning.”

	Titans of Innovation Roundtable

	Billy Parks, head of FOX creator studios, had a light bulb moment 15 years ago while working with AT&T. He realized allowing creators to use their voice and authentic audience relationship drove more engagement than prescribed talking points.

	Sean Atkins, CEO of Dhar Mann Studios, believes the marketing system is broken. “When you have creators who now have the same skill as the Super Bowl, the fact that they get a phone call that says, ‘Hey, would you stand up for 15 seconds and hold a Coca-Cola for $25,000?’ is ridiculous.”

	Christina Kothari, global head of consumer marketing at Reddit, recently tapped into the creator economy for a brand partnership for “Resident Evil.” Three Reddit creators were invited to a preview of the film and live Ask Me Anything with the director.

	“Creators often get invited to these premieres, and that’s important because they’re a media channel and they give you the reach that you need,” she said. “But to pair those creators with the really in-depth fans that have been building these communities on Reddit for years, created a really special environment, and the content that was captured there was so authentic and so fun.”

	“I’m really excited to find new ways to kind of partner with the fandoms on Reddit and bring them in real life together with creators with IPs that they love,” she added.

	Kothari is excited to find new ways to partner with young creators. Parks said he is inspired by young people and creators, two audiences he said are tapped in and challenging traditional approaches from media companies.

	The Creator Boardroom: Building Culture and Scaling Partnerships

	Jarret Myer, CEO at UPROXX Studios, said the creator economy is bigger than people think it is.

	“It’s studios, it’s artists, it’s creators that are all happening outside of the traditional Hollywood formation,” he said. “More and more these people are creating the monoculture moments that everyone is talking about. To me, missing out on that is missing out on the point of entertainment and culture.”
	

	Culture Genesis partners with “culture-shifting content creators” like YouTube streamer IShowSpeed. These creators are able to create moments of mass consciousness that Culture Genesis CEO Shaun Newsum called “mini Super Bowls.”

	Zach Miller, JesserCo president, challenged the traditional channels for advertisers: “Do you just want to spend the money on the traditional media channel that has always been the place to spend it, and cross your fingers and hope to find younger audiences there, or do you need to broaden your strategy and think about either swapping some of that spend on TV for digital channels that allow you to reach that audience, or at least expand the spend so that you reach your sort of core audience that you’ve been historically reaching on TV?”

	For Newsum, the next frontier continues to engage fandoms through creators on YouTube and leverage their audiences.

	The New Era of the TV Business

	Jeremy Helfand, global vice president and head of Amazon Prime Video advertising, said the television business is changing around personalization and accountability within advertising.

	For Josh Mattison, executive vice president of digital revenue pricing, planning and operations for Disney Advertising, it has never been more relevant that audiences are coming together around things that bring connection.

	“From a consumer perspective, or from a brand perspective, you want to follow fandom wherever people are watching, and they’re watching in more ways than ever,” he said.

	Puja Vohra, CMO and executive vice president of advertising sales at Fox Corporation, said people align around great content. She has seen advertisers consider how to capture the power of broadcast, precision of digital and flexibility of streaming.

	Vohra said the power of big television events is in the people: “That power of communal viewing, of being able to engage masses of people around a virtual couch, if you will, that is what leads to engagement and lean in, and you’re more receptive to messages.”

	Live entertainment remains important, and Mattison said the goal is to meet viewers where they’re at and build a daily habit with television.

	Behind the Business: Netflix Comedy and the Return of “A Different World”

	Laughs have always been important at Netflix, said Tracey Pakosta, vice president of comedy original series for the platform.
	

	“A Different World,” a sequel to the original sitcom hits Netflix on Sept. 24. Showrunner Felicia Pride brought the concept to the streaming service with a goal to modernize the look and feel of the show while staying true to much of the feeling from the original.

	Pride said that multihyphenate legend Debbie Allen, who spearheaded the original series, was “very clear that now is the time to hear from young Black America, and that felt like a charge I could get behind.”

	Along with Netflix and Allen, Pride worked to discover the tone of the sequel series. The project shot at HBCUs in Atlanta to achieve an authentic texture to the setting at the fictional Hillman College.

	“We wanted to be honest and truthful about life, but also be hopeful,” Pride said of the potential fan reactions to the season’s content.

	While the original series had 22 episodes per season, the sequel season debuts with 10, which Pakosta was excited about.

	“I think more is more always, but I also understand this cycle of streaming and the wanting to make the best version of that show,” she said. “A lot of times the story in the first season eight makes the most sense, and then there are other stories where 10 makes more sense.”

	Storytelling Vanguards

	Writer and comedian Joel Kim Booster has not felt a shift in the wake of box office hits like “Obsession,” and he is hesitant about the possibility.

	“It does always feel like in the wake of the success of things like ‘Obsession,’ a lot of the people at the top learn the wrong lessons and make decisions that may seem like they try to replicate the same thing without realizing that at the core of what made ‘Obsession’ a success was its originality, its purity in idea and story,” he said.

	Creator and showrunner Nick Antosca said the “Obsession” effect is real, but “it doesn’t get rid of the gatekeepers or the gates.” The success was made possible because Universal put marketing money behind it, he said.

	Kim Booster said it is important to recognize that the “Obsession” effect is localized to mid-budget horror movies. When asked what the antidote is, he said movies like “The Invite” and films made outside of the awards conversation.

	“Someone told me that the only way this movie that I’m talking about would be in theaters is if people felt like they needed to see it to be a part of the discourse around award season,” he said. “I hope that small little indie movies, little indie dramas can get made without needing to be nominated for an Oscar or at least an indie spirit.”

	When asked if he listens to feedback, actor and “In Your Dreams” host Owen Thiele said his podcast is a personal venture that has built parasocial relationships from fans and some notes are hard to tune out because those fans feel they have a reason to give a note.
	

	The panel also discussed where the speakers go for real inspiration. Antosca said he turns everything off and reads novels to feel less like “a sponge that’s squeezed into a rock” after months in production.

	Looking forward, the panel called for more representation in the industry. Antosca said he hopes more original and unexpected things will pop through. Musician, composer and music supervisor Este Haim said she wants to see more women hired to compose for shows, and Thiele wants to see more shows and movies that give queer Black leads fulfilling emotional arcs.

	(Pictured top: actor and “In Your Dreams” podcast host Owen Thiele, comedian and actress Lisa Gilroy, musician, composer and music supervisor Este Haim)

title: Javier Bardem to Star in Drama Series ‘The Spread’ at HBO From Bill Dubuque, Sean Sansiveri
description: In a highly-competitive situation, HBO has given out a straight-to-series order for the drama “The Spread” with Javier Bardem attached to star and e
body:
In a highly-competitive situation, HBO has given out a straight-to-series order for the drama “The Spread” with Javier Bardem attached to star and executive produce, Variety has confirmed. 

	The project hails from writers Bill Dubuque And Sean Sansiveri, who also executive produce alongside Bardem. This will be Sansiveri’s first credited TV writing role. Matthew Vaughn will direct and executive produce. Brad Weston executive produces for Makeready, with Ian Stratford and Michael Bloom of Topic Studios also executive producing. The series is a co-production between HBO and Fifth Season TV Studio. 
	

	The logline states, “Miami is turning paradise into power — Wall Street South — a subtropical collision of industry titans, elite hedge funds, staggering wealth, ruthless competition, sex, nightlife and fun on an industrial scale. Into this sun-soaked arena comes a visionary billionaire (Bardem) who collects the brilliant, the hungry and the dangerous, then turns their ambitions loose on the markets that power America. He chases something bigger: the power to shift the center of economic gravity to Miami — and decide how long the party lasts.” 


	“Having long wanted to set a scripted series in Florida, HBO couldn’t be more excited to explore the gilded chaos of Miami and bring it to life with this kaleidoscope of extraordinary, visionary talent who is as fearless as the story itself,” said Francesca Orsi, executive vice president of HBO Programming and head of HBO Drama Series and Films. 

	This marks the latest major series role for Bardem in recent years. He is fresh off the Apple TV adaptation of “Cape Fear,” in which he played the villainous Max Cady. He also recently starred in “Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story” at Netflix as Jose Menendez. He is primarily known for his film roles, which include his Oscar-winning turn in “No Country for Old Men,” as well as celebrated performances in films like the “Dune” franchise, “Being the Ricardos,” “Biutiful,” and “Before Night Falls.”
	

	He is repped by WME and Goodman Genow. 

	Dubuque is best known as the co-creator of the hit Netflix series “Ozark,” for which he shared in the show’s three Emmy nominations for outstanding drama series. He most recently created the crime drama “M.I.A” at Peacock, which is also set in South Florida, and executive produced the Netflix limited series “His & Hers,” which was also Fifth Season production. He is also known for writing films like “The Accountant” starring Ben Affleck and its sequel as well as “The Judge” starring Robert Downey Jr. and Robert Duvall. 

	He is repped by WME. Sansiveri is repped by CAA. 

	“‘The Spread’ is a gripping story of power and ambition, set against the vivid, glamorous backdrop of Miami,” said Noah Greenshner, executive vice president and head of TV Creative for Fifth Season. “We’ve brought together an exceptional creative team to capture the energy of this world and city, and we’re thrilled to be working alongside them and our partners at HBO, Makeready, and Topic to bring it to life.”

                          Couple Shares First Photos of Newborn
body:
McKenna West Surrogacy Scandal
                          Couple Shares First Photos of Newborn
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 18, 2026
                            2:12 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 18, 2026
                                2:55 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            The first photos of the baby at the center of the legal drama between the biological parents and surrogate McKenna West have been released ... and they are tough to look at.
      
    
            TMZ obtained two photos of the newborn from his biological parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, and the images show a long scar down the middle of his chest from emergency heart surgery.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The child, who Omar and Nausheen call Rumi, is hooked up to all sorts of tubes and machines monitoring his health. It's a lot to take in.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            McKenna, who calls the child Gabriel, refused to terminate the baby despite Omar and Nausheen wanting to do so after a heart issue was diagnosed during the pregnancy. The surrogate flew to Texas to give birth ... and has been involved in a legal battle with Omar and Nausheen for months over who will get the baby.
      
    
            The newborn is currently with Omar and Nausheen, as the parties wait for the Supreme Court to decide whether it will review the case. 
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Nausheen and Omar's lawyer, Lee Budner, tells TMZ, "While McKenna West has been conducting a publicity tour, Rumi's parents have been quietly caring for their child and following the recommendations of Rumi's medical team."
      
    
            Lee adds ... "[McKenna's] requested stay to the United States Supreme Court threatens the continuity of Rumi's medical care. A stay would not change who Rumi's parents are. It would only create confusion over medical decision-making authority and jeopardize the providers' ability to rely on the parents’ consent to Rumi’s treatment."

                          Alleged Sexual Assault Victim Wants Big $$$
body:
Trey Songz
                          Alleged Sexual Assault Victim Wants Big $$$
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 18, 2026
                            11:30 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Trey Songz's alleged sexual assault victim is pleading with the court to release a huge chunk of the money the singer paid to settle the matter ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Jauhara Jeffries said she settled her lawsuit in 2025 in which she claimed the singer sexually assaulted her.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She says the money is currently being held in a court-controlled escrow account until a lien issue is handled, but is asking the court to release 55% of the total amount or all amounts above $69,950.52. That means the settlement is at least around $70K, and she says she needs the money ASAP.
      

            The woman claims the delay is stopping her from being able to move on with her life. The court denied the request but set a hearing later this month.
      
    
            Jauhara sued Trey in 2021, claiming he sexually assaulted her at a Florida nightclub. She says she partied with Trey on January 1, 2018, at a New Year's Eve Party at Diddy's home and says Trey invited her to the club with other girls.
      
    
            At the club, she claimed Trey inserted his fingers into her vagina without consent. The woman said that despite the incident, she got into Trey's car later in the night.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The alleged victim claimed that during the car ride, Trey demanded she turn over her phone ... and when she refused, she said Trey had her forcibly removed from the vehicle.
      
    
            Trey adamantly denied the allegations.
